posts.author: Jim McPherson
posts.post_subject: Cheap source for 80mw Laser Diode and nice optics.
posts.content_md:
I've been looking for a cheap source for a high power laser diodes. Thor Labs and digikey sell the laser diode in DVD writers. I just bought a 16x DVD writer from newegg.com recently for $55.00 and free shipping, it works great. So I bought 2 more to pull the laser out of. I bought 16x writers, one was an AOPEN, the other was a Sony DW-D22A. The AOPEN had a samsung 4.8mm long can diode (12 pin, no feedback), the Sony had a SLD1236VL in a 5.6mm standard can diode. I use the Sony since it fits in common diode mounts. 

The SLD1236VL pdf can be found here:

[http://www.sony.net/Products/SC-HP/cx_n ... 1236vl.pdf](http://www.sony.net/Products/SC-HP/cx_news/vol37/pdf/sld1236vl.pdf)

That's 80mW CW, and it is single mode.

Not bad for $57.00 including the rest of the drive.

In addition I got 2 nice lenses, and a couple beam splitters in each drive.

If you like experimenting, this might be a good thing to try.

-Jim

posts.content_md:
I'm also in this boat and hope to stabilize one of these diodes.

I ended up going in on a group buy with a bunch of people. From Thorlabs if you buy 10 or more of these, the price drops to $41 the Mitsubishi ML120G21 80mw 658nm.

I have my diode, finally mounted in an temperature controlled, ILX Lightwave 4412 laser diode mount I picked up, from ebay of course.

I'm going to drive it with a low noise driver I bought from Wavelength Electronics, and cool it with a temperature controller from them also.

They claim this temperture controller can stabilize a load to .001 Degree C.

We'll See...

If any one is interested I think the group buy will happen again soon.

I have some pictures of my setup, but I just have to figure out how to post them.

-G

posts.post_subject: Cheap source for 80mw Laser Diode and nice optics.
posts.content_md:
> I'm going to drive it with a low noise driver I bought from Wavelength Electronics, and cool it with a temperature controller from them also.They claim this temperture controller can stabilize a load to .001 Degree C.We'll See...If any one is interested I think the group buy will happen again soon.I have some pictures of my setup, but I just have to figure out how to post them.

I use a direct current driver fom Roithner (EU-38 ) and i found no problems regarding current /wavelength stability, although the laser power is a bit less than battery operated diodes of low power.

I adapted a multi turn potentiometer into EU-38 for a precise current control in the diode, it works well, depending on the diode current limit, you need provide a resistor limiting current in serial with diode. The EU-38 output voltage is 4.5V, used only with **constant current mode.**

An aluminum heat sink is used as inertial heat control; with the help of a uncoated etalon, I see the interference fringes very stable, I think it will work.

.

posts.author: Jim McPherson
posts.post_subject: Cheap source for 80mw Laser Diode and nice optics.
posts.content_md:
It's good to hear that constant current is working. The driver I'm using is very similar to the EU-38. Frankly, I'm amazed that optical feedback works at all with holography. The idea of altering the beam tracking power ONLY and after it's already changed just gives me bad vibes. From my experiments so far, a well warmed up diode, at constant current (no photodiode feedback) is the most stable setup that I can do. One reason that I was looking for the sony diode specifically is that it is spec'd to operate at up to 75C. That means that I probably won't need a large heatsink and can use cheap (digikey) mounting hardware.

As soon as I get back from this trip I'll shoot a few quick single beams to see how it works out.

-Jim

> **tpark:** I have one of the Mitsubishi ML120G21 diodes, but I've not been able to get any good holograms out of it. I am driving it with a constant current driver, and I tried various different currents/holders, but I have not found a setup where I get a stable, hop free beam from this device. All the holograms I've made from this diode (Actually I have two of them) have sliced bread bands on them. Perhaps I'm doing something wrong though. I have early versions of this device, maybe later ones are better.

Mode hopping vary from diode to diode, model to model and even between units, you need to provide a smooth current control (with temperature stabilized) to "fly" the mode hope regions and map it for each diode. there are required regions of current value that mode hop will not occur.

At high current value for each diode, most of them will be relatively less prone to form mode hop's.

See [http://www.ilxlightwave.com/appnotes/mo ... lasers.pdf](http://www.ilxlightwave.com/appnotes/mode_hopping_semiconductor_lasers.pdf)

.

Yes - I read that application note, and its a good one.

I'm using a constant current supply which I use with the LNCQ05PS diode, and with that device it seems to be quite easy to find a spot where the diode behaves in a stable fashion. The 35mw mitsubishi diode seems to work well too, however the high power diodes that I have don't appear to stablilize properly. 

These diodes are from a fairly early run (I tried to order them from Thorlabs a while ago, and I had them call on first availability of the device) so they may not be as well behaved as later models of the device. I would be interested in hearing from anyone who has managed to get a good hologram from this diode. My testing/measurement facilities are somewhat limited. Perhaps someone with better hardware/measurement facilities could characterize these devices, but I have to do things the hack way.

posts.content_md:
Concerning the 80mW diodes, of course i tested them. They can work single frequency until 50mW about then they are multi-longitudinal mode until 80mW. They are not designed yet for single frequency operation at maximum power and will give fringed hoos. So until a new batch is available, better to use 50 or 60 mW diodes which can be fount single frequency.

[http://perso.wanadoo.fr/holographie/](http://perso.wanadoo.fr/holographie/)
